issues.issue: The indemnity covers "all liabilities, losses, damages, claims, costs and expenses ... arising out of or due to their actions or omissions" with no requirement that the acts be within the scope of the indemnitee's duties to the Trust. The only limit is the willful misconduct/gross negligence/fraud proviso, leaving the outer boundary of covered conduct unstated.

Advances and reimbursement are made available to "the Trustee, the Committee, or members of the Committee," but the clawback obligation on an adverse determination is imposed only on "the Trustee." By expressio unius the Committee and its members keep advanced funds even if their conduct was fraudulent, a gap on the face of the subsection.

This subsection limits the Trustee's indemnity to amounts "not covered by insurance, if any," which cannot be squared with Section 4.3(d)'s obligation to "periodically advance or otherwise reimburse on demand" the Trustee's expenses or with Section 4.3(c)'s unqualified indemnity. Whether advancement must await a coverage determination is left unresolved.

The statement that "any opinion of counsel shall be full and complete authorization and protection in respect to any action taken" gives absolute protection, which cannot be squared with Section 4.3(a)'s preservation of liability for willful misconduct, gross negligence and fraud. A court would have to decide whether counsel's opinion defeats the Section 4.3(a) exceptions.

Third parties may rely on the Trustee's authority "[i]n the absence of actual knowledge to the contrary" and need not inquire, which cannot be squared with Section 3.3(e)'s requirement of Committee approval for dispositions of assets worth $5,000 or more. Whether an unapproved sale binds the Trust depends on reconciling the two.

The second sentence is self-contradictory as drafted: the permissible investments "shall be limited to include only those investments, or shall be expanded to include any additional investments, as the case may be," without saying who decides which branch applies or when. The enumerated list in (a)-(c) may accordingly be either narrowed or enlarged by an unspecified mechanism.

This subsection sets fixed hourly rates and lets the Trustee raise them once a year on ten days' notice "without approval of the Bankruptcy Court," which cannot be squared with Section 3.3(d), under which compensation and reimbursement "shall be limited to the extent, and in the manner provided in, the Plan." Which instrument caps the Trustee's fees would have to be construed.

The subsection is conditioned on the Trustee being "unable to borrow funds ... in accordance with the terms of this Trust Agreement," but no provision of the instrument authorizes borrowing — Section 3.2's enumerated powers do not include it and Section 3.3(a) restricts activities to orderly liquidation. The condition presupposes a power the whole instrument never grants.

The temporal clause is garbled: the duty applies "while serving as Trustee under this Trust Agreement following the termination of this Trust Agreement or following the earlier of his or her removal or resignation," which describes a period that cannot exist. Whether confidentiality survives termination, removal or resignation turns entirely on repairing that sentence.

The closing relative clause has no clear antecedent — "unless the Bankruptcy Court otherwise determines or consents to an earlier effective date, which shall be the date that appointment of a successor Trustee becomes effective" leaves it unclear whether "which" refers to the earlier date, the proposed effective date, or the resignation generally. The date the Trustee's service ends is the thing left uncertain.

The section defines "Cause" in detail for removal by the Bankruptcy Court and then, in the next sentence, permits the Committee to remove the Trustee "without cause," which renders the Cause definition largely inoperative. Which removal route governs, and whether the Cause standard constrains the Committee at all, is unresolved on the face of the provision.

The acceptance instrument must be "in form satisfactory to the successor Trustee" — the very person executing it — so the requirement imposes no check by the Bankruptcy Court, the Committee or the outgoing Trustee. On its face the condition is circular and gives the successor sole control over its own qualification.

This section binds the Agreement to and for the benefit of the Trustee's "heirs, legal and personal representatives, successors or assigns," which cannot be squared with Sections 5.1 and 5.2, under which only the Bankruptcy Court or the Committee may appoint a successor Trustee. Whether the office can pass to an heir or assignee is the tension left open.

This section directs the Trustee to comply with, or qualify for exemption from, the Investment Company Act of 1940 if compliance is required, while Section 3.3(c) flatly forbids the Trust or the Trustee from taking "any action that would result in the Liquidating Trust becoming subject to registration" under that Act. The two provisions give contradictory instructions in the same event.

The annual holder statement is due only "[p]romptly following the end of each calendar year," a term that fixes no deadline and is measured against nothing else in the instrument. When the Trustee is in breach of the reporting duty cannot be determined from the words used.

The redistribution sentence turns on Trust Assets that are "not duly claimed," but no provision of the Agreement establishes any claiming procedure, deadline or notice against which "duly" could be measured. What forfeits a holder's distribution is therefore unstated.

The amendment power runs to "[a]ny substantive provision," a term left undefined and drawing a line between substantive and other provisions that appears nowhere else in the instrument. Which provisions the Trustee and Committee may alter — and who may alter the rest — cannot be determined from the section.

This section states that the Agreement "may be amended to comply with such federal income tax laws, which amendments may apply retroactively," naming no actor and no approval requirement, which cannot be squared with Section 8.1's requirement that amendments be made by the Trustee only upon Committee approval. Whether a tax-driven retroactive amendment needs Committee consent is left open.

The section vests in the Trust "[a]ny attorney-client privilege, work-product privilege or other privilege or immunity to which the estate or the Debtor are entitled" without distinguishing the Debtor's own privileges in matters unrelated to the Trust Assets. The reach of "the Debtor" as a privilege holder after the Effective Date is unstated.

The Debtor "shall relinquish to the Trustee all of its books and records" without qualification, exception or right to retain copies, in contrast to the reasonableness qualifiers governing the further-assurances sentence immediately before it. Whether records unrelated to the Trust Assets, or needed for the Debtor's own tax and corporate obligations, are covered is unaddressed.

The section applies California law "and federal bankruptcy law to the extent applicable" without saying which governs a conflict, and confers exclusive Bankruptcy Court jurisdiction only "[f]or so long as the Chapter 11 Case may be pending," naming no forum thereafter. Both the governing-law hierarchy and the post-closing forum are left unresolved.

The notice provision gives addresses only for the Trustee and for holders of Interests, omitting the Debtor and the Committee, both of which are parties to the Agreement and entitled to notices under Sections 3.3(f) and 9.3. By expressio unius there is no prescribed method of giving them notice.

This section incorporates the Plan and makes the Plan control over any inconsistent provision, which cannot be squared with Section 8.1's grant of power to the Trustee and Committee to amend or waive substantive provisions of this Agreement, since any amendment departing from the Plan would be void on adoption. The Plan is also amendable under the Preamble, so the controlling text can change after execution.
